headline: You're a methodical Go and PostgreSQL backend engineer who treats payment systems the way a structural engineer treats bridges: plan first, test first, ship in small pieces, and write the runbook.

archetype.name: The Ledger Keeper
archetype.description: You use AI the way a careful senior engineer uses a sharp junior colleague. You want the plan before the code, the reasoning before the diff, and the tests before the change. Your prompts are short and clear, they set boundaries like "step 1 only" and "do not touch the handlers yet", and they almost never need a correction. Your work centres on billing and ledger systems, where idempotency, isolation levels and rollback paths decide whether money goes missing. You care as much about the ADR, the runbook and the PR description as about the SQL itself.

dimensions.title: Plan, constrain, test, repeat
dimensions.summary: You usually start a task by asking for a plan, hypotheses or competing approaches. Then you split the work into small steps and limit what the AI may touch at each one. Tests come first in many sessions: characterization, integration, property-based, rollback and benchmark tests. Your sessions are short weekday-morning bursts, and each prompt builds on the one before.

evidence.quote: Before writing any code, outline a plan for adding idempotency keys to the payments API. List the risks.
Let's start with step 1 only: the database migration.
Keep it under 80 lines and add tests first.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.

dimensions.title: Terse, decisive, show-your-work
dimensions.summary: Your prompts are short and imperative, with a median of 85 characters and no small talk. You make clear calls ("Go with the dual-credential approach") and add an occasional "Please". You often ask the AI to explain its reasoning before it changes anything.

evidence.quote: Agreed, use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Show me the diff only.
Go with the dual-credential approach.
Can you explain why before changing anything?
Add alerting thresholds and explain how you chose them.

dimensions.title: Go + PostgreSQL, no ORM
dimensions.summary: You're a backend developer on billing and ledger services, working in Go with plain SQL through sqlc. You know PostgreSQL in depth, including isolation levels, locking and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Your test tooling includes testcontainers and rapid.

evidence.quote: Explain how this behaves under READ COMMITTED versus SERIALIZABLE.
Write the migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and a check that it is valid afterwards.
Please don't use an ORM here, plain sqlc queries.
Write the SQL and property-based tests with rapid.

dimensions.title: Correctness, money and operational readiness
dimensions.summary: You keep coming back to reliability in payment systems: idempotency, delivery guarantees, the outbox pattern and zero-downtime changes. You also put real effort into the work around the code, such as ADRs, design docs, runbooks with rollback sections, PR descriptions and reviewer assignment.

evidence.quote: Add a section about exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery and how consumers should deduplicate.
The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Run through the edge cases again: leap years, currency rounding, negative line items.
Suggest which reviewers should look at which files, based on risk.

dimensions.title: Thinking through trade-offs out loud
dimensions.summary: You use the AI as a sparring partner on design and concurrency. You ask for comparisons and guarantees before committing to a choice. The learning shows up as sharper decisions, not as tutorials.

evidence.quote: What are the trade-offs between using a mutex here and a channel?
What constraints guarantee that every transaction balances?
Propose two approaches and compare them.

traits.name: Plan-first
traits.description: You often ask for a plan, hypotheses or alternative approaches before any code gets written.

evidence.quote: Before writing any code, outline a plan for adding idempotency keys to the payments API. List the risks.
Help me form hypotheses before we look at code.
Propose two approaches and compare them.

traits.name: Scope fencer
traits.description: You set tight limits on each step so the AI can't wander off: one step at a time, PR-sized chunks, one concern per commit.

evidence.quote: Do not touch the handlers yet.
Now break the rollout into PR-sized steps.
refactor in small commits, one concern per commit, and tell me the commit messages first.

traits.name: Test-first by reflex
traits.description: Tests come before or alongside changes in many sessions, and they often target failure modes such as rollbacks.

evidence.quote: Implement step 1 of the outbox rollout: the outbox table and the transactional write. Tests first.
Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.
Add a benchmark so we can compare later.

traits.name: Reasoning auditor
traits.description: You want the AI to explain why before you accept what it changes.

evidence.quote: Can you explain why before changing anything?
Explain your reasoning step by step.
Add alerting thresholds and explain how you chose them.

traits.name: Paper-trail builder
traits.description: You treat ADRs, design docs, runbooks, checklists and issue templates as part of the deliverable.

evidence.quote: Document the decision in an ADR.
Sections: context, goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, rollout.
Turn the checklist into a GitHub issue template.

funFacts: Your correction rate is 0%: across 36 prompts, you never had to walk the AI back.
There's not a single prompt from Friday, Saturday or Sunday. Tuesday is your busiest day with 13.
26 of your 36 prompts landed between 09:00 and 11:00, so your coding with AI happens in the morning.
billing-service took 29 of your prompts and ledger got the other 7.
Your median prompt is 85 characters, roughly one terse, well-aimed sentence.
